title: Test how strong old bleach is
summary: Old bleach is weak, and dose charts assume the strength on the label. Mix a measured millilitre into a measured volume of clean water, read free chlorine with a pool kit, work out the real strength and scale the dose. Bleach burns eyes and skin, and mixed with ammonia, acids or toilet cleaners it gives off toxic gas.

materials.item: The bleach to test: plain, unscented
Pool or spa test kit that reads free chlorine (DPD)
1 mL or 5 mL syringe (first aid kit, pharmacy, vet supplies)
Clean pail and a measuring jug of known size
Clean chlorine-free water: distilled, bottled, or clear rain or meltwater

steps.text: Read the label: plain, unscented bleach only, and note the sodium hypochlorite percentage and the date code (EPA water, Clorox date).
steps.warn: Not scented, colour-safe, splash-less or with added cleaners (EPA water). Nothing else goes in the test water.

steps.text: Put on goggles and gloves and work where air moves.
steps.warn: Bleach burns eyes and skin (EPA bleach label). Never mix it with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or toilet cleaners: they give off toxic gas. See the chemicals card.

steps.text: Measure exactly 10 L (or 20 L) of the cleanest chlorine-free water you have into a clean pail, using a jug of known size. Test a sample: free chlorine must read zero.
Draw exactly 1 mL of bleach into a syringe, squirt it under the water surface and stir well.
Test free chlorine with a DPD pool kit, reading it on the kit's own timing (WHO TN11 describes the DPD comparator method).
If the colour is past the top of the chart, or oddly faint, dilute a sample 1 to 1 with the same clean water, test again and double the reading (Taylor FAQ).
Work out the strength: with 1 mL in 10 L, the reading in mg/L is the strength in percent. Otherwise, strength (%) = reading × litres ÷ (mL × 10) (IFRC jar test).

Compare with the label. Small differences mean nothing, because labels give sodium hypochlorite and kits read chlorine (EPA bleach label). A big shortfall, such as 6% bleach reading 3, means scale the dose.

Scale the dose: chart dose × chart strength ÷ your strength. From Health Canada's 0.2 mL per litre of 5.25% bleach, that is 10.5 ÷ your strength in mL per 10 L (HC emergency water). Double it for cloudy, coloured or very cold water (EPA water).

Clear cloudy water first: let it settle, then strain it through a clean cloth (EPA water). Treat the water, wait at least 30 minutes, and 1 to 2 hours if it is colder than 10 °C (HealthLinkBC disinfecting), then confirm at least 0.2 mg/L free chlorine as in [Test water with found kits](#guides/test_water) (WHO TN11, HC emergency water).
Write the tested strength and date on the bottle. Keep it capped, cool and dark, and test again after heat or months of storage (HC chlorate, Clorox date).

notes:
## Why test it
Every bleach dose chart assumes the strength on the label: Health Canada's 2 drops (0.2 mL) per litre is for 5.25% bleach (HC emergency water), and EPA's chart is for 6% or 8.25% (EPA water). Bleach doesn't keep that strength. Clorox says its bleach lasts up to a year if stored away from heat and direct sunlight; after that its breakdown into salt and water speeds up, until it is too weak to disinfect (Clorox date). EPA's emergency method calls for fresh bleach, or bleach kept at room temperature for less than a year (EPA water), and one EPA-accepted bleach label says plainly that it degrades with age, so use a chlorine test kit and increase the dose as needed (EPA bleach label). After a disaster, the bleach you find may well be older than a year, or have sat in a hot car or shed. A pool kit and 10 minutes tell you what you actually have.

## The arithmetic
A 1% solution holds 10 g of chlorine per litre, which is 10 mg in every millilitre. One millilitre of a 1% solution in 10 L of water gives 1 mg/L (IFRC jar test). Bleach works the same way, so:

**1 mL of bleach in 10 L of clean water gives about 1 mg/L of chlorine for every 1% of strength.** Fresh 6% bleach should read about 6 mg/L; bleach that reads 3 mg/L is about 3%.

For any amounts:

**strength (%) = reading (mg/L) × litres of water ÷ (mL of bleach × 10)**

| Bleach | Water | 1% of strength reads | Fresh 6% should read |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 mL | 10 L | 1 mg/L | about 6 mg/L |
| 1 mL | 20 L | 0.5 mg/L | about 3 mg/L |
| 5 mL (1 metric teaspoon) | 50 L | 1 mg/L | about 6 mg/L |

Pick the row that lands in the middle of your kit's scale. DPD reagent can bleach out above about 10 ppm and give a false low or zero (Taylor FAQ). Check where your kit's scale ends: the 20 L row suits a kit that tops out around 5.

Labels give strength as sodium hypochlorite; pool kits read chlorine. The two aren't quite the same: one label shows 7.5% sodium hypochlorite as 7.13% available chlorine (EPA bleach label). So small differences from the label mean nothing. What you are looking for is a big shortfall, such as a 6% bottle reading 3.

## Doing it well
- **Use the cleanest water you have, with no chlorine in it:** distilled, bottled, or clear rain or meltwater. Test it first: it must read zero. Water with dirt or organic matter in it uses chlorine up (its chlorine demand) (WHO TN11), which makes the bleach look weaker than it is.
- **Read it soon after mixing, on your kit's own timing.** The IFRC bucket test is built on water using up chlorine over its 30-minute wait, so the free chlorine left is less than what went in (IFRC jar test). A quick reading in clean water should stay closer to what you added (our reasoning).
- **Measure, don't count drops.** A 1 mL or 5 mL syringe from a first aid kit, pharmacy or vet supplies is best. The sources don't agree on what a drop is: Health Canada counts 2 drops as 0.2 mL (HC emergency water), HealthLinkBC counts 2 drops per litre of 5.25% bleach as 0.1 mL (HealthLinkBC disinfecting), while EPA's chart counts 16 drops as 1/4 teaspoon, about 1.2 mL, and 12 drops as 1/8 teaspoon, about 0.6 mL (EPA water).
- **Measure the water too:** a jug of known size into a pail, not a guess at the pail.
- **If the colour is past the top of the chart, or oddly faint,** dilute a sample 1 to 1 with the same clean water, test it, and double the result (Taylor FAQ).
- **Strips are rough:** good to about half the gap between two colour blocks (Taylor FAQ). Treat the answer as roughly right, not exact.

If anything goes wrong, it errs on the safe side: chlorine demand or a slow reading makes bleach look weaker, so you add a bit more. That is our reasoning, not a tested result, and it is why you still check free chlorine after treating.

## Scaling the dose
New dose = chart dose × chart strength ÷ your tested strength. Starting from Health Canada's 0.2 mL per litre of 5.25% bleach (HC emergency water), that is 2 mL per 10 L, and for weaker bleach:

| Your bleach tests at | mL per 10 L of clear water | mL per 20 L pail |
|---|---|---|
| 6% | 1.75 | 3.5 |
| 5.25% | 2 | 4 |
| 4% | 2.7 | 5.3 |
| 3% | 3.5 | 7 |
| 2% | 5.25 | 10.5 |
| 1% | 10.5 | 21 |

These are Health Canada's dose scaled by the arithmetic above. Double them for cloudy, coloured or very cold water (EPA water), stir, wait at least 30 minutes (HC emergency water), and longer in cold water: WHO says the contact time must be increased below 18 °C (WHO TN11), and HealthLinkBC says 1 to 2 hours below 10 °C (HealthLinkBC disinfecting). Then do the free-chlorine check in [Test water with found kits](#guides/test_water): at least 0.2 mg/L after the wait (WHO TN11, Health Canada chlorine TD). That check is the real proof, whatever the bottle says. Chlorine is ineffective against Cryptosporidium and removes no chemical contaminants, however well it is dosed (WHO TN11). Where either is a worry, boil the water as well (EPA water says boiling kills protozoa, but not chemicals) or use a cyst-rated filter, or find another source.

Hypochlorite stored a long time breaks down partly into chlorate (HC chlorate), so a big dose of very old bleach likely adds more of it than a small dose of fresh (our inference). Use the freshest bleach you can find, and keep weak bleach for cleaning if you have better.

## What weakens bleach
Health Canada says liquid hypochlorite must be protected from heat, light, a drop in pH and heavy metals (Health Canada chlorine TD), and that its breakdown in storage depends on pH, temperature, time, ultraviolet light, strength and traces of metals (HC chlorate). It tells water plants to use hypochlorite within 3 months of delivery and store it below 30 °C, out of sunlight (HC chlorate). One bleach label says every 5 °C cooler storage halves the rate its breakdown products form, and that diluting stronger solutions slows it significantly (EPA bleach label). So:
- A bottle from a cool, dark basement is likely better than one from a hot garage, a car or a sunny window.
- Stronger bleach (8.25%) may lose strength faster than regular bleach kept the same way (our inference: the label says only that dilution slows the formation of breakdown products, EPA bleach label).
- Read the date code: on Clorox bottles, a line on the neck starts with a plant code (a letter and a number), then the two-digit year and the day of the year (Clorox date).
- Bleach left in an unheated building over a Canadian winter: test it before you rely on it.
- Health Canada says solid forms of hypochlorite aren't affected by this decomposition (HC chlorate), and that calcium hypochlorite must be kept from heat, damp and organic material (Health Canada chlorine TD). The first sentence doesn't name pool shock, so applying it to dry pool shock is our reading. That makes it the better thing to stockpile (our inference). See [Shop chemicals](#ref/reference_chemicals/pool_chlorine_for_drinking_water).

## Other ways to know the strength
Pool and chemical suppliers sell bleach test kits that read strength directly. LaMotte's 7894-01, for example, gives available chlorine in percent by counting reagent drops on a diluted sample (LaMotte bleach kit). If you find one, use it the same way, then scale the dose.

Only plain, unscented bleach goes in drinking water: not scented, colour-safe, splash-less or with added cleaners (EPA water).
